title.en: Weaving: from nature's weavers to cloth

text.en: The male baya weaver builds a hanging, pouch-shaped nest from grass, weaving strands over and under. Young ones just learning make rough nests.

Weaving combines strips or threads into a patterned fabric. One set of threads runs vertically and the other horizontally, crossing over and under.
People have woven mats, baskets and sheets from coconut fibre, palm reeds, bamboo, grass, jute, cotton and silk.
Activity: weave paper strips of two colours over and under to make a mat. With threads instead of strips it becomes cloth. Look at a shirt through a magnifier to see the criss-cross pattern.
India knew how to weave 4,000 years ago. Weaving by hand on a loom gives handloom fabric. Examples: Kanjeevaram from Tamil Nadu, Pashmina from Kashmir and Ikat from Odisha and Gujarat.
The handloom sector employs over 45 lakh people, many of them women and rural artisans.
Weaving gives work to families and keeps traditional skills alive. Textile mills use machines to make cloth in large quantities.
Indian muslin was so fine that it was called woven air.
The Patola saree from Patan, Gujarat takes six months to a year to weave one saree.
